runtime semantics require more than the generic placement conventions.

## Ideal time-dependent RF cavity {#variable-rf-cavity-model}

`VARIABLE_RF_CAVITY` prescribes a uniform longitudinal electric field in its
straight element frame. Let $A(t)$ be the amplitude-model output in MV/m,
$f(t)$ the frequency-model output in MHz, and $\phi(t)$ the phase-model output
in radians, with $t$ and the integration variable $\tau$ in seconds. For
constant or polynomial frequency models, the implemented field is

$$
\mathbf E_{\mathrm{RF}}(\mathbf r,t)
=\widehat{\mathbf z}\,10^6 A(t)\,
\sin\!\left[2\pi\,10^6\int_0^t f(\tau)\,d\tau+\phi(t)\right]
\chi_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf r),
\qquad \mathbf B_{\mathrm{RF}}=0,
$$

in V/m and T respectively. The support indicator is one on

$$
\mathcal C=\{(x,y,z):\ 0\le z<L,\ |x|\le W/2,\ |y|\le H/2\},
$$

and zero elsewhere; $L$, $W$, and $H$ are the full cavity dimensions in metres.
The longitudinal entrance and both transverse faces are included, while the
longitudinal exit is excluded. The field is added to any existing external
and self-fields. Particle-loss apertures are a separate tracking operation.
The [input guide](../../user-guide/elements.qmd#element-time-dependence-definitions)
describes the available time models and current integral limitations.

This is an ideal prescribed-field buncher model, without an electromagnetic
cavity-mode solution, fringe fields, or transverse RF focusing. Within the
ordinary drift--kick--drift integrator, the device particle kernel and host
reference evaluate the field at the physical midpoint $t+h/2$ of each step
of duration $h$. Subdividing a step changes this sampling time consistently;
it does not reset the RF phase each turn. See the
[integration method](../overview/index.qmd#ring-boris-pic).

For constant amplitude $E_0=10^6A$ in V/m and angular frequency
$\omega=2\pi\,10^6f$ in rad/s, a particle with charge $q$ in C and approximately
constant speed $v$ through the cavity gains

$$
\Delta K \simeq q E_0 L\,
\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{\omega L}{2v}\right)
\sin(\omega t_c+\phi),
\qquad \operatorname{sinc}(u)=\frac{\sin u}{u},
$$

in joules, where $t_c$ is the time at the cavity centre. This finite transit-time
formula is a useful weak-kick approximation, not a replacement for integrating
the reference when its speed changes appreciably. A stationary synchronous
particle requires zero integrated energy gain and an RF frequency
$f_{\mathrm{RF}}=h_{\mathrm{RF}}/T_{\mathrm{rev}}$ in Hz, where $h_{\mathrm{RF}}$
is an integer harmonic and $T_{\mathrm{rev}}$ is its measured return time in
seconds. Choose the restoring phase using the ring's longitudinal dynamics
and calibrate the finite-cavity reference motion. A chosen phase alone does
not establish a self-consistent space-charge match.

The automatic maximum-energy cavity phaser does not change this element's
explicit phase model. `COF` remains a static magnetic, fixed-energy orbit
calculation; it does not solve the RF-periodic six-dimensional synchronous
orbit. Bare-orbit input and RF tracking must respect the
[orbit handover constraints](../../user-guide/tracking.qmd#opalx-initial-orbit).


## MONITOR sampling {#monitor-sampling-model}

::: {.feature-opalx}

`MONITOR` is a passive sampling plane, without a detector-material or field
model. The [input guide](../../user-guide/elements.qmd#monitor) describes its
collection modes, output files, and retained timestamp conventions.

### Spatial crossings

Let $\mathbf r=(x,y,z)$ and
$\mathbf u=\mathbf p/(mc)=\gamma\boldsymbol\beta$ be the particle state in
the monitor frame, with $\gamma=\sqrt{1+|\mathbf u|^2}$. For a positive
particle timestep $h_k$, the predicted displacement is

$$
\Delta\mathbf r_k=c h_k\frac{\mathbf u_k}{\gamma_k}.
$$

A crossing is recorded when $z_k<0$ and $z_k+\Delta z_k>0$. The linear
intersection fraction and sampled position are

$$
\lambda_k=-\frac{z_k}{\Delta z_k},\qquad
\mathbf r_k^{\mathrm{hit}}=\mathbf r_k+\lambda_k\Delta\mathbf r_k,
\qquad z_k^{\mathrm{hit}}=0.
$$

The strict inequalities exclude exact endpoint hits and reverse crossings.
The saved momentum is $\mathbf u_k$, without a momentum update at the
intersection. In ordinary drift--kick--drift tracking, the stored crossing
time is calculated as

$$
t_k^{\mathrm{hit}}=t_b+\frac{h}{2}+\lambda_k h_k,
$$

where $t_b$ is the bunch time at the start of the step and $h$ is the bunch
timestep. This is a straight-drift estimate from the sampled state, not an
additional integration through external or self-fields. Particle positions,
momenta and crossing times are collected over the passage, rather than at one
common laboratory time.

### Temporal snapshots

A temporal snapshot is triggered by the reference particle's crossing.
For an ordinary full timestep $h>0$, let $t_m=t_{\mathrm{end}}-h/2$ and
$(\mathbf r_{\mathrm{ref}},\mathbf u_{\mathrm{ref}})$ be the reference state
supplied at the midpoint. Define

$$
\tau=-\frac{z_{\mathrm{ref}}}{h v_{\mathrm{ref},z}},\qquad
t_{\mathrm{cross}}=t_m+\tau h,
\qquad
\mathbf v_{\mathrm{ref}}=c\frac{\mathbf u_{\mathrm{ref}}}
{\sqrt{1+|\mathbf u_{\mathrm{ref}}|^2}}.
$$

The snapshot origin is placed at the predicted reference intersection and its
longitudinal axis is aligned with the reference momentum. If $\mathcal T$
is the rigid transform from the current container frame to that snapshot
frame, and $Q$ its rotation, the sampled positions are

$$
\mathbf r_k^{\mathrm{snapshot}}
=\mathcal T(\mathbf r_k^{\mathrm{end}})
+\left(\tau-\frac12\right)h\,Q\mathbf v_k.
$$

Thus each particle is drifted by the same time correction from the timestep
endpoint. Longitudinal particle offsets are retained: this is a bunch
snapshot, not an intersection of every particle with $z=0$. The calculation
uses a rigid spatial transform and straight drift, without a Lorentz boost
or an additional momentum push. The saved momentum is the current container
momentum.

The current output stores $t_{\mathrm{cross}}$ as reference `TIME`, but
$t_{\mathrm{end}}$ as each particle's `time`. Accordingly,

$$
\texttt{meanTime}-\texttt{TIME}
=\left(\frac12-\tau\right)h
$$

for an ordinary full step. The two agree when $\tau=1/2$ and generally differ
otherwise. This timestamp convention is distinct from the time used to drift
the snapshot positions; see the
[output interpretation](../../user-guide/elements.qmd#monitor-output-times).

:::
